Tarnogrod Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Tarnogród, Poland

Not demolished. Tarnogród, founded in 1567 under Magdeburg Law, initially barred Jewish settlement under pressure from Christian residents in 1569 before lifting the ban in 1580; kehilla facilities followed shortly after. Jewish population peaked at 51% (3,733 of 7,287 residents) in 1906, still 44% by 1939. The cemetery, founded in 1580 (possibly 1588), held a mortuary and three ohels; Germans completely destroyed it in 1941 and paved roads with its tombstones. During the 1942 ghetto liquidation, Nazis shot roughly 1,500 Jews near the Catholic cemetery, about 3,000 more near Kościuszki Street, and additional victims directly at this cemetery site, all in unmarked mass graves; survivors were deported to Bełżec. Between 1985-1990, the American Schorer and Scheiber families funded a full restoration - fencing, a recovered-matzevot lapidary, and memorials at all three execution sites.
